title: Together Compiler: Continual Compilation for AI inference
gist: Together AI introduces Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven continual optimization loop for inference that uses persistent engines to cut engine start from 467s to 9s and reports up to 2.6x higher TPS, 1.7x over megakernels, and record low-latency InferenceX results. The post argues inference is now polymorphic and must be re-optimized as traffic drifts.

insights.claim: Inference workloads are too varied to hand-optimize: none of the top-10 open-source LLMs on OpenRouter share an architecture, Together serves many trillions of tokens per day across thousands of customers, and hardware spans H100, B200, B300, NVL72, VR and Groq.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Architecture and hardware fragmentation favors automated, per-workload optimization and undercuts static kernel moats.
insights.quote: none of the top-10 open-source LLMs on OpenRouter use the same architecture!

insights.claim: Traffic shifts materially over time: one country's working-hours traffic had 1.4x longer prompts than another's (97k vs 70k), prompt length rose 80% two weeks after a model release as users moved to agentic workloads, and bursts can double prompt lengths and drop cache hit rates.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Agentic usage drives longer contexts and burstier traffic, changing inference cost structure.

insights.claim: The author claims agents are well suited to searching the optimization space without fixed heuristics, but today's agentic systems are bottlenecked by the speed of experimentation.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Experiment throughput, not agent intelligence, is the binding constraint on agent-driven kernel and system optimization.

insights.claim: Existing agentic optimizers relaunch engines like VLLM, SGLang or TRT-LLM for each experiment, with start times of tens of minutes; TKCC uses persistent engines that hot-reload candidate forward passes, cutting total time to serving from 467s to 9.0s.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: A roughly 50x faster experiment loop is the core technical edge claimed.
insights.quote: engine start times are tens of minutes

insights.claim: TKCC claims 252x higher experiment throughput than baseline agentic performance optimization systems.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Throughput of experimentation is presented as the source of its gains.

insights.claim: TKCC uses a two-tier engine setup, with fast engines loading a few layers for rapid, low-variance timing and slower engines loading many layers to test optimizations on real data distributions, because MoE and sparse attention make input data distributions change which optimization wins.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Benchmarking kernels on random inputs can mislead for data-dependent architectures.

insights.claim: TKCC uses a custom cost model combining hardware specs, microbenchmarks and measured forward passes to select parallelism strategies (TP, EP, DCP), arguing spec-based picks miss effects like MoE expert imbalance and uneven prompt lengths, and that the best layout shifts with concurrency.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Raw hardware spec comparisons understate real-world deployment differences across chips.

insights.claim: In under 24 hours TKCC achieves up to 2.6x higher TPS across frontier open-source models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek v4.1-Flash) versus highly optimized baselines on SemiAnalysis' AgentX workloads, per Together's own evaluation.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Self-reported software gains on existing GPUs can lower cost per token without new hardware.

insights.claim: TKCC sets a state-of-the-art for low-latency batch-size-1 inference on InferenceX at 1111 TPS on MiniMax M3.1-Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1-Flash, using its cost model's parallelism choice rather than the InferenceX configuration.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Vendor-reported records; they position Together at the latency frontier for agents.

insights.claim: TKCC outperforms available open-source megakernels by 1.7x on the canonical Llama 1B batch-size-1 workload, on both H100 and B200, a setting that human experts and traditional ML compilers have already heavily optimized.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Agent-generated optimization beating hand-tuned kernels on a mature benchmark suggests broad headroom.

insights.claim: TKCC finds larger speedups than Claude Code with the /goal command on three of four models from weather modeling, PDE, time-series and biology codebases, and Together uses it as a general-purpose AI compiler beyond LLM inference.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Specialized optimization loops may beat general coding agents for systems work.

insights.claim: Together says TKCC is already serving trillions of tokens in production.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Claims production deployment rather than a research demo.

insights.claim: Together argues inference is now 'polymorphic', with traffic constantly and dynamically evolving much like financial markets, making polymorphic AI systems the next systems frontier.
insights.speaker: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
insights.so_what: Inference providers' edge may shift from fixed engines to continuous adaptation capability.
insights.quote: Polymorphic AI systems is the next frontier
insights.locator: Polymorphic AI systems is the next frontier

source_meta.author: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, and Simran Arora
